Baigana podaବାଇଗଣ ପୋଡ଼ା

Roasted garlic or raw additions; flame or broiler.

By Ahimanikya Satapathy

Meet the dish ↗

A taste to remember. A question to take with you.

Begin the story ↓
Further readingFootnotes & Sources
On this page
Further readingFootnotes & Sources

Pragyan suggests putting garlic into slots in the eggplant before roasting. After peeling and mashing, roasted garlic, onion, ginger, cream and green chilli are added. The account also offers an oven alternative: this is one cook’s preparation, not a regional formula.1

Away in the Kitchen recalls a mother roasting eggplant and tomato over a flame. The writer adapts that preparation to a broiler, describing it as familiar but not smoky. The peeled vegetables are mashed with uncooked onion, garlic and chilli, then finished with mustard oil.2

The photograph shows combined eggplant and tomato, baigana-bilati poda. It is not a photograph of either recipe described here.

entries.text: document.getElementById('journey-data').textContent="{\"catalog\":[{\"id\":\"reading:stories/maniabandha\",\"title\":\"Maniabandha: Where Odisha’s Weaving Heritage Meets a New Generation of Travellers\",\"author\":\"Ahimanikya Satapathy\",\"kind\":\"Reading\",\"area\":\"Cuttack\",\"summary\":\"In this village in Cuttack district, the future of textile tourism depends on understanding the skill behind the sari—and keeping its makers at the centre.\",\"href\":\"/stories/maniabandha/\",\"checked\":\"2026-10-29\",\"practical\":[{\"heading\":\"\",\"text\":\"A patterned sari begins long before the cloth takes shape. In the weft ikat tradition associated with Maniabandha, the design is planned in yarn: sections are bound, colour is applied, and the prepared threads are woven into a pattern. What a buyer sees as a finished motif begins as a series of decisions about placement, colour and alignment.\"},{\"heading\":\"\",\"text\":\"That process offers a compelling reason to visit Maniabandha, a weaving village in the Badamba area of Odisha’s Cuttack district. The district’s export action plan describes the village and neighbouring Nuapatna as a region of concentrated weaving activity, working predominantly in cotton, with silk also present. Here, a textile can become an introduction to the people and knowledge behind its making.\"},{\"heading\":\"\",\"text\":\"The craft is commonly known in Odisha as bandha. Unlike a design printed onto finished fabric, ikat is created by resist-dyeing yarn before weaving. In weft ikat, the pattern is carried by the crosswise threads. The work demands coordination between preparation and weaving: the design must remain intelligible as separate lengths of coloured yarn become cloth. Tata Trusts’ documentation of Maniabandha shows yarn preparation and dyeing as part of a wider household craft economy, drawing attention to work that is easily overlooked when only the finished sari is displayed.\"},{\"heading\":\"\",\"text\":\"Maniabandha’s cultural setting adds another dimension. Odisha Tourism describes a village shaped by Buddhist and Hindu communities, with textiles featuring motifs such as lotus flowers, elephants and lions. These traditions invite careful interpretation. A motif may carry different meanings for different makers; hearing a weaver explain a design can be more revealing than assigning every pattern a single religious meaning.\"},{\"heading\":\"\",\"text\":\"The neighbouring weaving centres also belong to the wider story of Khandua textiles and the Jagannath tradition. The Development Commissioner (Handicrafts)’ GI compendium records Nuapatna’s historic connection with cloth woven for the deities at Puri and includes Maniabandha Weavers’ Cooperative Society among the registration holders for Khandua Saree and Fabrics. This connection places the region’s weaving within a continuing relationship between craft and worship.\"},{\"heading\":\"\",\"text\":\"The names deserve precision. Khandua’s existing GI recognition should not be confused with the separate application for “Maniabandhi Saree.” As checked on 29 October 2026, the latter remained at the examination stage in the official GI registry. Recognising the relationship between these textile traditions need not erase their distinct identities.\"},{\"heading\":\"\",\"text\":\"Maniabandha’s appeal has received national recognition. It was among the winners in the crafts category of the Ministry of Tourism’s Best Tourism Villages Competition in 2024. Odisha Tourism now presents the village as a destination for watching weaving, meeting makers and purchasing textiles directly. The recognition offers a chance to bring the work of its artisans to a wider audience.\"},{\"heading\":\"\",\"text\":\"Preparing artisans to welcome visitors has also been part of Odisha’s wider approach. In September 2022, The New Indian Express reported that the Handlooms, Textiles and Handicrafts department had enlisted IITTM faculty for a proposed training programme covering 730 artisans and entrepreneurs across 73 handloom clusters. An initial group of 80 weavers from four districts, including Cuttack, had received hospitality and soft-skills training. This is evidence of a statewide initiative; it does not establish a new or continuing Maniabandha-specific course.\"},{\"heading\":\"\",\"text\":\"The question of where tourism happens matters to the community. On 6 January 2026, The New Indian Express reported that weavers represented by the Maniabandha Handloom Cluster Consortium opposed locating the proposed Maniabandha Buddhist Handloom Village Tourism Centre in nearby Abhimanpur. They wanted it established in Maniabandha itself. The report also recorded the district collector’s position that the centre would be built in Abhimanpur. The disagreement concerns a proposed facility, and should not be read as evidence that a completed centre is open to visitors.\"},{\"heading\":\"\",\"text\":\"The issue carries a wider lesson for craft tourism: location influences which households visitors meet, where they spend and whose account of a place they hear. A successful project needs the participation of the people whose work gives it meaning.\"},{\"heading\":\"\",\"text\":\"There is relevant experience in artisan enterprise. Tata Trusts includes Maniabandha among the clusters supported by Antaran, its craft livelihoods programme. Its approach combines design education, business skills, pricing, communication and connections with buyers. These are practical foundations for tourism too: an engaging demonstration has greater value when the artisan can set its terms, explain the product and retain a fair return.\"},{\"heading\":\"\",\"text\":\"The craft is also finding new ways to make its provenance visible. In its August 2026 magazine, Tata Trusts describes an Antaran pilot with technology company Kosha across three weaving clusters, including Maniabandha. Loom sensors and QR labels help connect participating textiles to information about their making. The programme’s account also acknowledges practical challenges, from tagging fabric that will later be cut to artisans’ concerns about designs being copied online. The pilot suggests a useful direction: buyers should be able to learn who made a textile and understand what they are paying for.\"},{\"heading\":\"\",\"text\":\"For travellers, a thoughtful visit begins with an arrangement rather than an expectation that every working household is open to the public. Ask before entering or photographing, agree on any demonstration fee, and allow time for the maker’s explanation. When buying, ask about the fibre, technique, care requirements and who made the piece. Such questions help turn a purchase into an informed appreciation of labour and skill.\"},{\"heading\":\"\",\"text\":\"For Maniabandha, the most useful measure of tourism will be what it contributes to weaving households: paid time, worthwhile orders, stronger customer relationships and opportunities for younger artisans. A visitor who understands how a pattern takes shape may leave with more than a sari. They may leave knowing whose work they want to support again.\"}],\"sources\":[{\"title\":\"Cuttack district export action plan\",\"url\":\"https://eodbodisha.odisha.gov.in/Upload/DEAP/CTT.pdf\"},{\"title\":\"Antaran textile catalogue\",\"url\":\"https://www.tatatrusts.org/upload/pdf/antaran-product-catalog.pdf\"},{\"title\":\"Tata Trusts’ photographic 2026\",\"url\":\"https://horizons.tatatrusts.org/2026/august/tata-trusts-horizons-advantage-artisans.html\"}],\"aliases\":[],\"planningArea\":\"Cuttack\",\"access\":\"A reading idea, not a scheduled visit.\"},{\"id\":\"reading:stories/odia-dhaga\",\"author\":\"Ahimanikya Satapathy\",\"title\":\"The Poetry We Speak: Why Odia Dhaga Matter\",\"kind\":\"Reading\",\"area\":\"Odisha\",\"summary\":\"Odia sayings carry images, humour and ways of judging everyday life.\",\"href\":\"/stories/odia-dhaga/\",\"practical\":[{\"heading\":\"The Poetry We Speak\",\"paragraphs\":[\"“ଅତି ଲେମ୍ବୁ ଚିପୁଡ଼ିଲେ ପିତା ।” Squeeze a lemon too much, and it turns bitter.\",\"A small sentence, an ordinary fruit, a familiar action. Yet the thought travels well beyond the kitchen. We can press a request until goodwill gives way to resentment. We can pursue one more advantage until we spoil what we already have. The saying brings those possibilities into view through something we can almost taste.\",\"This is one of the pleasures of Odia Dhaga. A thought arrives with a picture inside it. The listener participates: lemon becomes insistence, bitterness becomes the consequence, and an everyday action becomes a way of examining our conduct. In that movement from one experience to another, we encounter the work of literature.\",\"I have lived outside Odisha for thirty-five years. The language and the life it carries have stayed with me. My concern now is how we help that connection continue for someone else. When an expression stops passing between people, we stand to lose more than a sentence. We may lose a particular way of noticing, teasing, consoling or questioning.\",\"Grammar helps us understand how a language is put together. Living with a language also teaches us what people can do with it: how an image changes an argument, how a pause makes a joke, how affection or anger alters the same words. Dhaga offer a particularly vivid entrance into that life.\"],\"text\":\"“ଅତି ଲେମ୍ବୁ ଚିପୁଡ଼ିଲେ ପିତା ।” Squeeze a lemon too much, and it turns bitter. A small sentence, an ordinary fruit, a familiar action. Yet the thought travels well beyond the kitchen. We can press a request until goodwill gives way to resentment. We can pursue one more advantage until we spoil what we already have. The saying brings those possibilities into view through something we can almost taste. This is one of the pleasures of Odia Dhaga. A thought arrives with a picture inside it. The listener participates: lemon becomes insistence, bitterness becomes the consequence, and an everyday action becomes a way of examining our conduct. In that movement from one experience to another, we encounter the work of literature. I have lived outside Odisha for thirty-five years. The language and the life it carries have stayed with me. My concern now is how we help that connection continue for someone else. When an expression stops passing between people, we stand to lose more than a sentence. We may lose a particular way of noticing, teasing, consoling or questioning. Grammar helps us understand how a language is put together. Living with a language also teaches us what people can do with it: how an image changes an argument, how a pause makes a joke, how affection or anger alters the same words. Dhaga offer a particularly vivid entrance into that life.\"},{\"heading\":\"Poetry before we call it poetry\",\"paragraphs\":[\"In The Question That Brought Me Here, I wrote about encountering poetry before identifying it as poetry: through a melody, a memorable voice, or a story that enters family conversation. Dhaga invite a similar encounter. A listener can enjoy the sound or recognise the situation before asking what kind of literature it is.\",\"Consider this expression:\",\"ବଣ ପୋଡ଼ିଲେ ଦୁନିଆ ଜାଣେ, ମନ ପୋଡ଼ିଲେ କେହୀ ନ ଜାଣେ\\n\\nWhen the forest burns, the world knows; when the heart burns, no one knows.\",\"The two halves hold the same shape. ବଣ and ମନ draw forest and inner life close through sound; the repeated burning carries us from a visible blaze to pain that may remain unseen. The second half changes what we understand from the first. “No one knows” gives the feeling its force, without requiring us to believe that care or understanding is impossible.\",\"Here is compression, parallelism and metaphor working together. A private feeling becomes imaginable through a public scene. We do not need to turn every saying into a formal poem to recognise its literary power.\",\"The joke and the judgement often arrive together. Three expressions show how much can happen between the picture we first recognise and the thought we carry away.\",\"A family word becomes a practical question\",\"ନାହିଁ ମାମୁଁ ଠଉଁ କଣା ମାମୁ ଭଲ\\n\\nA one-eyed maternal uncle is better than no maternal uncle.\",\"The repeated word mamu places the comparison within a family. We are invited to imagine someone to whom we might turn, rather than an abstract quantity of help. The sentence moves quickly from absence to possibility: something useful may still be available even when it is not everything we hoped for.\",\"Its blunt comparison can carry a teasing, rueful voice. Beneath that voice is a question we meet repeatedly: do we wait for the ideal, or make thoughtful use of what is within reach? A small borrowed room may let a reading group begin. It need not be the room they hope eventually to have. The saying makes room for a beginning; it does not require us to accept every bad arrangement.\",\"The bodily comparison also carries a prejudice we should recognise. Disability is not a measure of a person's worth. We can understand the practical thought while choosing a kinder image when we speak to someone.\",\"Praharaj's Purnnachandra Odia Bhashakosha records the saying and explains it through the care an uncle might offer a nephew. It also places other-language equivalents beside it. This is a printed witness within the dictionary's 1931–1940 publication series, not an account of who first made the saying.\",\"The feet outside the hiding place\",\"ଲୁଚିଛି ନା ଗୋଡ ଦିଇଟା ଦିଶୁଛି!\\n\\nAre you hiding? Your two feet are showing!\",\"The scene is already a joke. Someone thinks they have disappeared; the listener can still see their feet. The words for hiding and showing echo one another while pulling in opposite directions. The contradiction makes the line easy to hear and remember.\",\"It can describe a transparent excuse, an unsuccessful pretence or a secret whose clues remain in view. Imagine someone concealing a surprise parcel while its bright wrapping sticks out of the bag. The humour comes from the distance between what the person believes they have achieved and what everyone else can see.\",\"That distance gives the joke its deeper question: what do we fail to notice about ourselves? We may attend carefully to our intentions and scarcely at all to the signs we leave behind. The saying offers a quick way to puncture that confidence. Used affectionately, it lets someone laugh at the gap; used harshly, it can humiliate. Nor does a suspicious-looking clue, by itself, establish guilt.\",\"A March 2012 Aahwaan editorial uses a related form while discussing literature and politics, recalling it as an expression heard in childhood. Here we can see a saying doing work in literary discussion: a visible bodily image becomes a way to question a public appearance. The recollection does not date its first use.\",\"The wood that answers back\",\"ମୋତେ ଯେତେ ମାଠିବୁ ମାଠ ମୁହିଁ ସେଇ ଦରପଡ଼ା କାଠ\\n\\nPolish me as much as you like; I remain that half-burnt wood.\",\"This time the object speaks through a person. Someone's attempt to polish or improve the speaker meets a comic refusal: keep trying; I am still myself. The repeated polishing and the sound of ମାଠ against କାଠ make the answer feel compact and conclusive.\",\"There may be affection in such a reply, or exasperation, or a joke at one's own expense. Its meaning changes with the occasion. Is the speaker resisting needless pressure to become fashionable? Or using a familiar line to escape advice worth hearing? The same witty answer can protect independence or shelter stubbornness.\",\"That is where the life of the saying becomes interesting. It gives us a voice, but it cannot make our judgement for us. We can enjoy the stubborn wood and still ask whether this is a moment to stand firm or to learn. Remembering the line is one thing; recognising the difference is another.\",\"These are proverbs and idiomatic expressions, not interchangeable rules or necessarily formal poems. Their literary force comes through different means: a family comparison, a comic scene, a speaking object, an answering sound. Each makes a thought easier to carry, while leaving us responsible for how we use it.\"],\"text\":\"In The Question That Brought Me Here, I wrote about encountering poetry before identifying it as poetry: through a melody, a memorable voice, or a story that enters family conversation. Dhaga invite a similar encounter. A listener can enjoy the sound or recognise the situation before asking what kind of literature it is. Consider this expression: ବଣ ପୋଡ଼ିଲେ ଦୁନିଆ ଜାଣେ, ମନ ପୋଡ଼ିଲେ କେହୀ ନ ଜାଣେ\\n\\nWhen the forest burns, the world knows; when the heart burns, no one knows. The two halves hold the same shape. ବଣ and ମନ draw forest and inner life close through sound; the repeated burning carries us from a visible blaze to pain that may remain unseen. The second half changes what we understand from the first. “No one knows” gives the feeling its force, without requiring us to believe that care or understanding is impossible. Here is compression, parallelism and metaphor working together. A private feeling becomes imaginable through a public scene. We do not need to turn every saying into a formal poem to recognise its literary power. The joke and the judgement often arrive together. Three expressions show how much can happen between the picture we first recognise and the thought we carry away. A family word becomes a practical question ନାହିଁ ମାମୁଁ ଠଉଁ କଣା ମାମୁ ଭଲ\\n\\nA one-eyed maternal uncle is better than no maternal uncle. The repeated word mamu places the comparison within a family. We are invited to imagine someone to whom we might turn, rather than an abstract quantity of help. The sentence moves quickly from absence to possibility: something useful may still be available even when it is not everything we hoped for. Its blunt comparison can carry a teasing, rueful voice. Beneath that voice is a question we meet repeatedly: do we wait for the ideal, or make thoughtful use of what is within reach? A small borrowed room may let a reading group begin. It need not be the room they hope eventually to have. The saying makes room for a beginning; it does not require us to accept every bad arrangement. The bodily comparison also carries a prejudice we should recognise. Disability is not a measure of a person's worth. We can understand the practical thought while choosing a kinder image when we speak to someone. Praharaj's Purnnachandra Odia Bhashakosha records the saying and explains it through the care an uncle might offer a nephew. It also places other-language equivalents beside it. This is a printed witness within the dictionary's 1931–1940 publication series, not an account of who first made the saying. The feet outside the hiding place ଲୁଚିଛି ନା ଗୋଡ ଦିଇଟା ଦିଶୁଛି!\\n\\nAre you hiding? Your two feet are showing! The scene is already a joke. Someone thinks they have disappeared; the listener can still see their feet. The words for hiding and showing echo one another while pulling in opposite directions. The contradiction makes the line easy to hear and remember. It can describe a transparent excuse, an unsuccessful pretence or a secret whose clues remain in view. Imagine someone concealing a surprise parcel while its bright wrapping sticks out of the bag. The humour comes from the distance between what the person believes they have achieved and what everyone else can see. That distance gives the joke its deeper question: what do we fail to notice about ourselves? We may attend carefully to our intentions and scarcely at all to the signs we leave behind. The saying offers a quick way to puncture that confidence. Used affectionately, it lets someone laugh at the gap; used harshly, it can humiliate. Nor does a suspicious-looking clue, by itself, establish guilt. A March 2012 Aahwaan editorial uses a related form while discussing literature and politics, recalling it as an expression heard in childhood. Here we can see a saying doing work in literary discussion: a visible bodily image becomes a way to question a public appearance. The recollection does not date its first use. The wood that answers back ମୋତେ ଯେତେ ମାଠିବୁ ମାଠ ମୁହିଁ ସେଇ ଦରପଡ଼ା କାଠ\\n\\nPolish me as much as you like; I remain that half-burnt wood. This time the object speaks through a person. Someone's attempt to polish or improve the speaker meets a comic refusal: keep trying; I am still myself. The repeated polishing and the sound of ମାଠ against କାଠ make the answer feel compact and conclusive. There may be affection in such a reply, or exasperation, or a joke at one's own expense. Its meaning changes with the occasion. Is the speaker resisting needless pressure to become fashionable? Or using a familiar line to escape advice worth hearing? The same witty answer can protect independence or shelter stubbornness. That is where the life of the saying becomes interesting. It gives us a voice, but it cannot make our judgement for us. We can enjoy the stubborn wood and still ask whether this is a moment to stand firm or to learn. Remembering the line is one thing; recognising the difference is another. These are proverbs and idiomatic expressions, not interchangeable rules or necessarily formal poems. Their literary force comes through different means: a family comparison, a comic scene, a speaking object, an answering sound. Each makes a thought easier to carry, while leaving us responsible for how we use it.\"},{\"heading\":\"Culture lives in the occasion\",\"paragraphs\":[\"The wording matters, but so does the moment in which it is spoken. The lemon saying could be a gentle reminder to ourselves. Directed sharply at someone asking for help, it could become a rebuff. Knowing the words does not settle whether their use is generous, fair or appropriate.\",\"Learning an expression therefore involves learning a relationship: who can say it to whom, in what tone, and with what possible effect. The hiding feet can prompt shared laughter; the stubborn wood can end a conversation that needed to continue. A translation can explain the picture. A conversation helps us understand its place.\",\"This is what I mean by culture embedded in language. The fruit, the fire, the family word and the wood that answers back give us more than vocabulary. They offer ways of making experience shareable. A saying lets a speaker approach a difficult thought indirectly; a listener may recognise the point, laugh at it, resist it, or turn it back on the speaker.\",\"In Odia Cultural Identity and Pride, I argued that pride grows through familiarity—through names we can use, stories we understand and skills we can practise. Dhaga give that thought a modest, practical beginning. That concern is a reason to listen and make room for them; it is not a survey of how all Odia families speak. Different households, generations and places will have different experiences. We should hear those differences before telling a single story of loss.\",\"A collection helps us keep wording and sources available. Continued use asks something more of us. Who will explain the joke? Who remembers another version? Who can show a learner why a line is tender in one setting and cutting in another?\",\"The picture may be what stays with us first: feet beneath a hiding place, a piece of wood under a polishing hand. Later, a new situation can bring the words back with a meaning we had not noticed before. We may recognise our own stubbornness where we once laughed at someone else's. A remembered saying can become a companion to judgement as we grow, without having the same lesson for every age or occasion.\",\"There is also a printed history to investigate carefully. A version of the lemon saying appears in the 1893 ଢଗମାଳିକା, ପ୍ରଥମଭାଗ, whose title page identifies Gobinda Rath as publisher and Victoria Press, Cuttack. That is evidence of the expression in print by that date. It does not tell us who first said it, and the publisher’s name should not become an invented author’s name.\",\"Keeping such distinctions is part of caring for the inheritance. Dhaga fit naturally into that kind of gathering. Read one aloud. Explain the literal picture. Invite someone to describe an occasion when it might be used. Let another person suggest an occasion when it would be unfair or unhelpful.\",\"A child’s objection can be a good beginning. Does more effort always spoil a result? Of course not. The lemon saying asks us to consider proportion; it does not relieve us of judging the situation. A learner who questions its use is already thinking with the language.\",\"At home, a small word notebook could keep the expression beside the name of the person who shared it and their account of when they would say it. With permission, a recording could preserve their pronunciation and rhythm. If another person knows a different version, keep that beside it rather than correcting it away without investigation.\",\"Older expressions also deserve judgement. Familiarity and age cannot excuse cruelty or prejudice. We can study an inherited expression while choosing not to use it against someone. Passing on culture includes showing how to question what we inherit.\",\"Project Odisha’s Words We Carry collection (https://projectodisha.org/dhaga/) brings together 201 illustrated expressions with Odia and English explanations and source notes. It offers a place to begin reading and listening. The next step can be small: choose one saying, hear its sound, consider its image, and bring it into a conversation where it belongs.\",\"I want a learner to feel the pleasure of that discovery—the moment when familiar words reveal another meaning, or a short line holds more life than its length suggests. That pleasure gives us a reason to return. The compact pairing gives difference a shape we can recognise. Learning how things are done elsewhere begins with attention, without requiring us to accept every practice uncritically. Imagined occasion: At a gathering in another town, a visitor asks how guests usually take part before assuming they match home. 24. Distance makes things look better ଦୂର ପର୍ବତ ସୁନ୍ଦର; ଦୂର ବନ୍ଧୁ ସୁନ୍ଦର A distant mountain is beautiful; a distant friend is beautiful. ଅର୍ଥ: ଦୂରରୁ ଦେଖିଲେ ପାହାଡ଼ ଓ ବନ୍ଧୁ—ଉଭୟଙ୍କ ଦୁର୍ବଳତା ଲୁଚିଯାଇପାରେ। ନିକଟରୁ ଜାଣିଲେ ଚିତ୍ରଟି ବଦଳିପାରେ। Both may look simpler before we encounter their rough edges. The parallel invites affection with clearer sight, not the conclusion that friendship is better kept remote. Imagined occasion: Someone envies a friend’s apparently effortless life until they hear about the work behind it. 25. Do not laugh at another’s turn ଉପର ବରଡ଼ା ଖସୁଛି,\\nମଝି ବରଡ଼ା ହସୁଛି \\nତଳ ବରଡ଼ା କହୁଛି,\\nମୋ ଦିନ କାଳ ଯାଉଛିରେ ଭାଇ ତୋ ଦିନକାଳ ଆସୁଛି ॥ The upper leaf falls; the middle leaf laughs; the lower leaf says, “My time is passing, brother; your time is coming.” ଅର୍ଥ: ଅନ୍ୟର ଅବସ୍ଥା ବଦଳିବା ଦେଖି ହସିବା ପୂର୍ବରୁ ନିଜ ପାଳି କଥା ଭାବିବାକୁ ଏହା ମନେ ପକାଏ। ସମୟ କାହା ପାଇଁ ଅଟକି ରହେନାହିଁ। The leaves fall, laugh and speak. This editorial reading hears a warning in their exchange: another person’s turn is not separate from our own passage through time. The changing voices make the reflection memorable without settling a botanical explanation or an original occasion. A payment record includes Khandayats among foot soldiers, alongside a cowherd sub-chief and three Muslim fort watchmen. Military musicians and other workers also supported the establishment. The connection with Khandayat is real; the record also shows why the two names cannot simply replace each other. Tanabe explains that military and administrative positions could become hereditary, carrying entitlements to land and payment. Access by people of different backgrounds did not mean equality: ranks and remuneration differed sharply. This offers a historical mechanism for inherited service identities, rather than a story of a single ruler creating one caste for one purpose. The surviving records discussed here establish a working institution by the late eighteenth century. They do not identify its first founder. It also discusses Paiko and Kottia Paiko as regional community names. Those passages preserve different uses of a related term; they are not permission to merge every community carrying it. The gazetteer also repeats older colonial classifications. Such records help trace how officials described people, but claims about ancestry, social rank or community character need critical checking and present-day community testimony. Jagabandhu’s own dispossession made his grievance especially visible. Khordha’s history describes Kandhas arriving from Ghumsur in March 1817 and Paikas joining them under Jagabandhu. The sequence matters: tribal participants were actors in the uprising, not merely a supporting crowd added to someone else’s story. The Government of India’s bicentenary account describes the rebellion spreading to Puri, Pipli, Cuttack and other places, with participation beyond the militia. It identifies Baxi Jagabandhu as the hereditary military chief and records British suppression after the initial rebel successes. Khordha’s cultural account describes village groups performing Paika Nrutya, a battle dance, during Dussehra. It names dholak, nagara, shehnai and dhak as accompaniment. The district account relates the word Paika to padatika, meaning infantry. This is a locally documented connection between martial memory, performance and the festival calendar; it does not establish an unbroken choreography from the eighteenth century. To understand an akhada in its own place, begin with the people who sustain it. What do they call their practice in Odia? Who taught them, which occasions bring them together, and what has changed between generations? A named teacher, a remembered training place and a carefully described movement can make heritage more tangible than a sweeping claim of antiquity. For family and community histories, keep the same care: record the place, the period, the name people use for themselves and the evidence behind an origin account. An inherited story deserves to be heard in its own words. Yumiko Tokita-Tanabe’s fieldwork among Khandayat women in Garh Manitri, Khurda, ran from April 1991 to November 1992. Her study describes women preparing household and ancestral offerings, including food and water. Domestic work and ritual knowledge also sustained belonging; this evidence comes from a particular village and period. The same study records turmeric and oil used in a first-menstruation bathing ritual. Turmeric use therefore has a documented local setting. This does not establish the history of today’s staged wedding “Haldi” ceremony: the occasion, form and transmission of a custom matter as much as its ingredients. Washing at a birth or funeral brought two seers of rice and 25 paise. The same study says Pano and Kolha families were excluded from the service. Collected leaves are sun-dried for two or three days, then five or six are joined with thin bamboo slivers to make a plate. Plates are bundled for sale. The account also identifies October–February as a local peak in leaf quality and availability. That description makes the finished plate less anonymous. Drying, joining and preparing it for sale are separate tasks, not something a leaf does by itself. The plate carries a sequence of decisions about material, preparation and the form in which it will reach a buyer.\",\"paragraphs\":[\"The Balliguda Forest Division working plan for 2021–22 to 2030–31 describes siali as a woody climber with large leaves. Buyers assess holes, dryness and size; plates move through local traders, with some later trimmed or pressed. It distinguishes hand stitching, sewing-machine stitching and press-moulded products. The material is shared, but the work and finished forms differ. The report also records pressures that a celebration of craftsmanship could overlook: limited drying and storage space, and urgent cash needs that can lead to distress sales. Its proposed improvements are not evidence that those improvements happened. A plant-based plate alone tells us neither whether its maker was fairly paid nor whether harvesting was sustainable.\",\"paragraphs\":[\"A February 2017 JICA report follows a Kandhamal siali chain beyond collection. Its title may appear in a bibliography, its author may be celebrated, and a copy may remain somewhere in a private collection. Yet a reader who wants to read the work may have no practical way to find it.\",\"href\":\"/stories/odia-literature-preservation/\",\"checked\":\"2026-11-04\",\"practical\":[{\"heading\":\"Odia Bibhaba and the Work of Keeping Literature Available\",\"paragraphs\":[\"Odia Bibhaba’s Pathagara addresses that distance between remembering literature and being able to read it. Its entrance leads to newspapers, magazines, books, reference works and collected writings. Dictionaries and bibliographies sit alongside literary collections. This breadth matters: a language’s written life includes the tools people used to understand it, as well as the poems and stories they made with it.\"],\"text\":\"Odia Bibhaba’s Pathagara addresses that distance between remembering literature and being able to read it. Its entrance leads to newspapers, magazines, books, reference works and collected writings. Dictionaries and bibliographies sit alongside literary collections. This breadth matters: a language’s written life includes the tools people used to understand it, as well as the poems and stories they made with it.\"},{\"heading\":\"How a science project became an archive\",\"paragraphs\":[\"The group behind Odia Bibhaba is Srujanika. Its account traces the preservation effort to science writing in Odia: collecting articles and examining dictionaries for terminology led it to Gopal Chandra Praharaj’s Purnachandra Odia Bhasakosha and to the difficulty of finding old publications.\",\"Srujanika dates Project Rebati to 2004 and the digital Bhasakosha to 2006. It describes homemade imaging equipment, open-source software and a see-through scanner for thick volumes. Before an archive becomes a website, somebody has to find a workable way of copying the book. Its later compilation of Odia periodicals from 1856 to 1950 included chronological and author indexes—tools for finding writing within the pages.\",\"The institutional history also needs its dates. In a post dated 23 May 2021, Srujanika said its digitisation work had ended and that work had begun at SOA’s PPRACHIN using its equipment and experience. It said it would continue managing the website for the time being. This records a transition; it does not establish the present arrangement or mean that the online collection closed.\"],\"text\":\"The group behind Odia Bibhaba is Srujanika. Its account traces the preservation effort to science writing in Odia: collecting articles and examining dictionaries for terminology led it to Gopal Chandra Praharaj’s Purnachandra Odia Bhasakosha and to the difficulty of finding old publications. Srujanika dates Project Rebati to 2004 and the digital Bhasakosha to 2006. It describes homemade imaging equipment, open-source software and a see-through scanner for thick volumes. Before an archive becomes a website, somebody has to find a workable way of copying the book. Its later compilation of Odia periodicals from 1856 to 1950 included chronological and author indexes—tools for finding writing within the pages. The institutional history also needs its dates. In a post dated 23 May 2021, Srujanika said its digitisation work had ended and that work had begun at SOA’s PPRACHIN using its equipment and experience. It said it would continue managing the website for the time being. This records a transition; it does not establish the present arrangement or mean that the online collection closed.\"},{\"heading\":\"Preserving the conversation around a work\",\"paragraphs\":[\"Old magazines preserve a different kind of literary history from a collected edition. An issue places writing beside other writing. Its contents, sequence and publication date can help a reader follow the discussion in which a poem, essay or story first circulated. Odia Bibhaba’s magazine introduction draws attention to the role of periodicals in debate and in the development of writers. It also describes the difficulty of locating surviving issues.\",\"For a reader, the value lies in being able to return to particular publications. A general statement about the richness of Odia literature becomes a more useful invitation when it leads to something one can open and read.\",\"The Gopal Chhotray collection offers one such route. Its catalogue brings together plays, one-act plays, operas, collected works, translations and material labelled as unpublished manuscripts. It lists a 1974 edition of Srimati Samarjani, which the collection identifies as Chhotray’s opera adaptation of Fakir Mohan Senapati’s Patent Medicine. It also lists his translation Natasamrat in a 1994 edition.\",\"Together, these entries suggest questions worth pursuing in the works themselves. How does a short story change when it becomes musical theatre? What happens when a play travels into another language? A useful archive allows the reader to move beyond an author’s reputation towards the forms, editions and relationships that make up a writing life.\"],\"text\":\"Old magazines preserve a different kind of literary history from a collected edition. An issue places writing beside other writing. Its contents, sequence and publication date can help a reader follow the discussion in which a poem, essay or story first circulated. Odia Bibhaba’s magazine introduction draws attention to the role of periodicals in debate and in the development of writers. It also describes the difficulty of locating surviving issues. For a reader, the value lies in being able to return to particular publications. A general statement about the richness of Odia literature becomes a more useful invitation when it leads to something one can open and read. The Gopal Chhotray collection offers one such route. Its catalogue brings together plays, one-act plays, operas, collected works, translations and material labelled as unpublished manuscripts. It lists a 1974 edition of Srimati Samarjani, which the collection identifies as Chhotray’s opera adaptation of Fakir Mohan Senapati’s Patent Medicine. It also lists his translation Natasamrat in a 1994 edition. Together, these entries suggest questions worth pursuing in the works themselves. How does a short story change when it becomes musical theatre? What happens when a play travels into another language? A useful archive allows the reader to move beyond an author’s reputation towards the forms, editions and relationships that make up a writing life.\"},{\"heading\":\"More ways to keep Odia literature in circulation\",\"paragraphs\":[\"Odia Bibhaba belongs within a wider effort to keep Odia literature available to readers and listeners. Recite World, Odia Wikisource and Odia Virtual Academy offer different ways to encounter that literature, hear its words and return to its texts.\",\"Recite World brings listening into this picture. Its own account identifies it as a programme of the Bhubaneswar-based Udaygiri Foundation Trust, intended to make Odia literary heritage accessible through listening and reading. It gives particular importance to dramatisation, pronunciation and encounters with unfamiliar words.\",\"Its page for Fakir Mohan Senapati’s Patent Medicine brings together an author introduction, a story description inviting the visitor to listen, and a PDF link. The title connects with the Gopal Chhotray adaptation catalogued by Odia Bibhaba. A reader can therefore approach the same literary work through a story presentation and the record of its transformation for the stage.\",\"This adds another dimension to preservation: a voice can draw attention to rhythm, dialogue and humour, inviting someone to return to the written work. A recorded reading is also an interpretation. Its performer and recording deserve their own credits alongside the writer and the edition used.\",\"Odia Wikisource shows how preservation can continue beyond the scan. Its page for Fakir Mohan Senapati’s Rebati presents the story as readable Odia text, with editing history and links to reading formats. A Wikimedia account published in January 2015 describes work on Bhagabata that included converting legacy-font text, proofreading and formatting. This was work on the usability and accuracy of the words, as well as their availability.\",\"The project also makes unfinished work visible. Its scan-linked index for the 1901 Barnabodha has numbered pages and a status indicating that the file needs checking. Such signals help readers distinguish a text that is available from one whose checking is complete.\",\"Odia Virtual Academy provides another entrance to Odia material. Its stated remit includes books, journals, manuscripts and archival records. Its novel catalogue offers discovery by title and author and lists works such as Antima Jatra and Matimatala. This is useful to a reader who knows a writer’s name but needs help finding a work. A catalogue listing, however, should not be mistaken for a guarantee that every linked file is complete or searchable.\",\"These collections can overlap. A scan may travel between a digitising group, a hosting institution and a volunteer transcription project. Recognising each contribution gives a clearer account of the work than treating every website as an entirely separate rescue of the same book.\"],\"text\":\"Odia Bibhaba belongs within a wider effort to keep Odia literature available to readers and listeners. Recite World, Odia Wikisource and Odia Virtual Academy offer different ways to encounter that literature, hear its words and return to its texts. Recite World brings listening into this picture. Its own account identifies it as a programme of the Bhubaneswar-based Udaygiri Foundation Trust, intended to make Odia literary heritage accessible through listening and reading. It gives particular importance to dramatisation, pronunciation and encounters with unfamiliar words. Its page for Fakir Mohan Senapati’s Patent Medicine brings together an author introduction, a story description inviting the visitor to listen, and a PDF link. The title connects with the Gopal Chhotray adaptation catalogued by Odia Bibhaba. A reader can therefore approach the same literary work through a story presentation and the record of its transformation for the stage. This adds another dimension to preservation: a voice can draw attention to rhythm, dialogue and humour, inviting someone to return to the written work. A recorded reading is also an interpretation. Its performer and recording deserve their own credits alongside the writer and the edition used. Odia Wikisource shows how preservation can continue beyond the scan. Its page for Fakir Mohan Senapati’s Rebati presents the story as readable Odia text, with editing history and links to reading formats. A Wikimedia account published in January 2015 describes work on Bhagabata that included converting legacy-font text, proofreading and formatting. This was work on the usability and accuracy of the words, as well as their availability. The project also makes unfinished work visible. Its scan-linked index for the 1901 Barnabodha has numbered pages and a status indicating that the file needs checking. Such signals help readers distinguish a text that is available from one whose checking is complete. Odia Virtual Academy provides another entrance to Odia material. Its stated remit includes books, journals, manuscripts and archival records. Its novel catalogue offers discovery by title and author and lists works such as Antima Jatra and Matimatala. This is useful to a reader who knows a writer’s name but needs help finding a work. A catalogue listing, however, should not be mistaken for a guarantee that every linked file is complete or searchable. These collections can overlap. A scan may travel between a digitising group, a hosting institution and a volunteer transcription project. Writing about the February 2013 Konark Dance and Music Festival, reviewer Lalitha Venkat describes Prativa from Bhawanipatna with a vocalist and two main drummers. Read within that limit, it shifts attention from the finished object to the obligations and institutions surrounding its maker.\"]},{\"heading\":\"When spelling had consequences\",\"text\":\"For Srinibasa Moharana, the difference between “Badhei” and “Badhai” was consequential. His application for an OBC certificate was refused on that distinction. How were their boats built? And could an older migration lie behind the maritime story? Follow the objects, the craft and the competing explanations.\",\"href\":\"/stories/maritime-memory/\",\"checked\":\"2026-10-17\",\"practical\":[{\"heading\":\"Begin with a question\",\"text\":\"A little boat carrying a lamp is a powerful way to remember a voyage. To understand the world behind it, we also need to look at a broken bowl, a fitted plank and the changing wind. Each reveals a different part of the crossing—and each belongs to its own time.\"},{\"heading\":\"Begin with the boat we remember\",\"text\":\"Boita Bandana sets small boats carrying lamps afloat; Bali Jatra in Cuttack commemorates Odisha’s maritime connections with Southeast Asia. They bring the ocean voyage into the scale of a household and a riverbank. But remembrance, a trading port and a prehistoric migration are different kinds of history. We cannot give them one departure date. Nor can we assume that “boita” names a single ship design used unchanged across centuries. The most revealing story begins when we ask what each piece of evidence actually preserves.\"},{\"heading\":\"A question to carry\",\"text\":\"What does your family place in its little boat, and what meaning does that act have for you? A household memory need not speak for every household.\"},{\"heading\":\"The merchants were part of an exchange\",\"text\":\"The trade was more than taking local produce away to sell. At Khalkattapatna, beside the Kushabhadra estuary, Rudra Prasad Behera’s 2016 ceramic study describes imported porcelain and celadon bowls and plates alongside locally made pottery. Chinese coins were also reported. These objects make the receiving shore visible: goods reached Odisha as well as leaving it. Manufactured goods belong in the picture too. Book II, chapter XI of the Arthashastra lists Kalinga among regions whose cotton fabrics were highly valued. This is evidence for the reputation of a product, not a surviving bill of lading showing that a particular cloth sailed to Bali. A textile reference and a medieval ceramic assemblage cannot simply be combined into the cargo of one timeless Sadhaba ship. “Exchange” also needs care. Imported objects establish circulation; they do not tell us whether a transaction used barter, money, credit or a gift. A coin at a port does not settle the payment method for every sale. Goods could pass through several merchants and ports. The evidence here supports a connected trading network, while individual contracts, prices, profits and return cargoes still need documentation.\"},{\"heading\":\"A question to carry\",\"text\":\"Could this object have reached the port through an intermediary? What would distinguish a direct voyage from a chain of exchanges?\"},{\"heading\":\"An anchor connects two Indian coasts\",\"text\":\"A broken stone anchor from Manikapatna, on the Chilika coast, adds a connection beyond the familiar Odisha–Bali pairing. In 2022, Sila Tripati and colleagues examined its rock through petrography, chemical analysis and isotopes. Basalt near Palitana in Gujarat emerged as the most likely source. The rock gives the story a material starting point. It does not identify the ship’s owner or crew, prove where the anchor was made, or draw every stage of its journey. Even the tools of voyaging could travel through networks. To recover one voyage, we would need evidence that joins its vessel, date, people and cargo.\"},{\"heading\":\"A question to carry\",\"text\":\"Which is being traced here: the rock, the anchor, or the vessel? Those journeys may be related without being identical.\"},{\"heading\":\"People crossed the sea as well as objects\",\"text\":\"I. Wayan Ardika and Peter Bellwood’s Sembiran research connects Indian traders with Bali through archaeological finds. That India–Bali connection matters, but the published abstract does not assign every Indian object to Odisha. Bali had its own communities and histories; it was a participant in exchange, not an empty destination waiting for visitors. A different kind of evidence comes from Angkor Borei in Cambodia. A study published in 2022 found South Asian ancestry in a child buried at the Vat Komnou cemetery, directly dated to 78–234 CE. This is evidence that contact could involve families and ancestry, not just objects moving between markets. The study does not identify an Odishan parent, a merchant occupation or the boat that made the crossing. Keep the distinction: goods can travel without their makers, and ideas can be learned without a population moving wholesale. A shared motif, a religious practice or a similar-sounding word needs its own dated history. The strongest account of cultural exchange asks who encountered whom and how something changed in the receiving community, rather than treating resemblance as a certificate of origin.\"},{\"heading\":\"A question to carry\",\"text\":\"What evidence would show people moving, rather than an object or an idea passing from hand to hand?\"},{\"heading\":\"There was no single boat for every water\",\"text\":\"The evidence discussed here includes no complete excavated Sadhaba ship from which to draw an exact construction plan. Medieval images offer fragments of the equipment. A Ratnagiri Tārā relief, assigned a late-eighth-century date in the scholarship discussed by Tripati and colleagues, depicts a mast, supporting stays and a steering oar. No sail is shown. The scene concerns rescue from maritime danger; it is not a shipyard drawing. Later craft studies let us examine actual construction traditions. Tripati’s 2015 chapter distinguishes the nauka of Chilika, the padhua associated with surf work, and the patia of the northern coast. In its nauka account, planks are fastened with wooden dowels and iron nails and seams are caulked with cotton. The padhua description instead has stitched planks, a flat bottom and no keel or frames. It is paddled and steered with a large stern oar. That padhua was used for beach-seine fishing and, historically, transfer between shore and larger vessels. Such work explains why a small coastal boat belongs in maritime history without turning it into an ocean-going Bali trader. These are later documented practices: they help us understand the range of solutions, but do not prove which arrangement an ancient merchant’s ship used.\"},{\"heading\":\"A question to carry\",\"text\":\"Was a boat intended to cross a lagoon, negotiate surf, work an estuary or sail offshore? Ask about its task before judging its shape.\"},{\"heading\":\"A plank becomes part of a hull\",\"text\":\"Swarup Bhattacharyya’s patia study follows builders along the Odisha–West Bengal coast. The owner specifies a length; other dimensions follow in proportion. Planks are heated and bent with a wooden device called merry kath. The hull takes shape before its internal floor and side timbers are fitted: this is shell construction. The patia combines reverse-clinker, carvel and clinker joints in different parts of the hull—different ways of overlapping planks or meeting their edges. Builders check symmetry with string, fasten the wood with nails and seal seams with cotton. Bhattacharyya also records fisherman Arjun Behera’s explanation that lighter arjun timber makes smaller boats easier to drag ashore. The account connects a material choice to the work of landing a boat. These details put skill back into the maritime story. The person fitting a joint must judge a curve, a gap and a material, then correct the work. Practical knowledge deserves attention in its own right. It need not be dressed up as a lost mathematical formula, or projected unchanged into antiquity, to be impressive.\"},{\"heading\":\"A question to carry\",\"text\":\"Look at the seam between two boards: how is it joined, sealed and supported? That small detail can tell you more than the size of the boat.\"},{\"heading\":\"The cargo changes the boat\",\"text\":\"A floating boat displaces water whose weight balances the total weight it carries: hull, equipment, people and cargo. Add a load and the hull sits deeper. This is the modern buoyancy explanation. It helps us understand the builder’s problem without claiming that an ancient crew used the equations in a modern physics textbook. Consider the consequence. More cargo leaves less height between the water and the edge of an open hull. A boat that floats in calm water is not thereby ready for waves. Weight distribution, the shape of the immersed hull, sound joints and the ability to keep water out all matter. These are engineering questions for any reconstruction; without a securely identified hull and loading arrangement, an exact ancient carrying capacity would be guesswork. The merchant’s wish to carry more and the crew’s need to preserve a margin against swamping therefore belong in the same conversation. So do food, drinking water and repair equipment: necessities have weight too. We have not recovered a Sadhaba provisioning list or a measured safety margin, and should not supply one from imagination.\"},{\"heading\":\"A question to carry\",\"text\":\"When a model is labelled with a cargo capacity, what measurements and loading assumptions support that number?\"},{\"heading\":\"The return journey had a season\",\"text\":\"A voyage needed a way home. Tripati and L. N. Raut’s 2006 study reconstructs an outward season using the northeast monsoon and a return season using the southwest monsoon. They relate wind and circulation patterns to historical accounts and festivals. This is an explanation of how seasonal travel could work, not a recovered timetable proving that every ship departed on one festival morning. Wind and current do different jobs: a sail responds to air, while a current carries the surrounding water. A helpful seasonal wind does not make every coastal approach or strait favourable. Waiting, choosing an approach and understanding local depth belong beside the long crossing. Knowing which way to head is different from knowing whether a loaded vessel can clear a shallow entrance. Kartika Purnima also invites a tidal question. Around full and new moons, the tidal range is generally larger: high waters are higher and low waters lower. That is the physical principle explained by NOAA. It does not establish a universal rule that all heavy ships launched on Kartika’s full moon. The local channel, timing, weather and depth still matter. The ritual calendar is evidence of remembrance; a historical launch rule requires its own evidence.\"},{\"heading\":\"A question to carry\",\"text\":\"What did a navigator need to know for the whole crossing, and what could only be learned about a particular harbour entrance?\"},{\"heading\":\"Could an older migration lie behind the story?\",\"text\":\"There is a serious maritime migration hypothesis worth examining. In 2019, linguists Felix Rau and Paul Sidwell proposed that a small group speaking an ancestor of the Munda languages reached the Mahanadi delta from Southeast Asia around 3,500–4,000 years ago. In their model, interaction with people already living there helped form Proto-Munda, which later spread inland. Their case combines language geography, reconstructed agricultural vocabulary and changes in word structure that they interpret as evidence of language contact. Their conference slides also acknowledge that the proposed early archaeological connection is more tentative and less securely dated than later maritime contacts. This is a model to test, not a named voyage. The authors leave the Southeast Asian departure point uncertain. Genetics supplies another kind of evidence. Kai Tätte and colleagues’ 2019 study of 102 Munda speakers estimated South Asian–Southeast Asian admixture between roughly 2,000 and 3,800 years ago for the sampled populations. “Admixture” means ancestry from previously differentiated populations coming together. A genetic estimate does not identify a landing beach, ship or festival. Present-day populations used as statistical comparisons are not automatically the actual ancient migrants. The wider population history remains debated. Debashree Tagore and colleagues’ 2021 analysis proposed much older shared ancestry between Indian and Malaysian Austroasiatic-speaking populations, followed by separation and later population changes. It also acknowledged missing ancient genomes from central and northeastern India. Its estimated population split and the 2019 study’s admixture dates describe different processes; they should not be presented as two dates for the same voyage. Linguist John Peterson, in an author-posted study, separately challenges the restricted prehistoric distribution assumed for Munda, arguing for a wider spread into the eastern Gangetic plains. None of this establishes that Odisha’s tribal communities arrived together on Sadhaba trading boats. “Munda languages” is a linguistic grouping, not a synonym for every tribal community in Odisha. The proposed prehistoric crossing, the much later objects at medieval ports, and the living Boita commemoration occupy different timelines. A connection between them is an important research question; it has not been demonstrated by the evidence reviewed here.\"},{\"heading\":\"A question to carry\",\"text\":\"Which question is a study answering: language history, ancestry, a migration route, a trading voyage or the history of a ritual? A strong connection must bridge those questions with evidence.\"},{\"heading\":\"Bring three questions to Jobra\",\"text\":\"Let this reading change how you look at a museum. Our Jobra guide is a place to begin planning; these questions are an invitation to notice, not a promise about today’s exhibits. What am I looking at: an original object, a model, or a later reconstruction? What date and place does its label give—and whose work made it possible? Beside the museum’s basket of cocoons, imagine tracing one strand forward. If you meet someone working with Tasar, ask which stage they know best. Can they show the difference between the cocoon, the prepared yarn and the finished fabric? Tasar identifies a silk material; it does not by itself tell you the weave, blend, dye, finishing or treatment of the cocoons. If those details matter to you, ask for evidence for this particular piece. Notice the sewing machine in Andrew Moore’s photograph. “Made by hand” here means attending to the maker’s work and decisions; it is not a promise that every stitch is hand-sewn. Ask which stages the person does and which tools they use. For the lampshade in the documented process, rings help give the stitched fabric its form. Ask a maker to show you one decision—a repeated shape, an edge or the way a piece holds its shape—if they have time. One well-chosen question can reveal more than a rushed tour of everything.\"},{\"heading\":\"From celebration to everyday objects\",\"text\":\"Odisha Tourism connects Pipili appliqué with the decoration of Jagannath’s chariots during Ratha Yatra. Ask what this object was made for, where its pattern came from and whether the maker gives it a particular name. Confirm an exact meeting point, opening arrangements, steps, seating and toilets with your chosen host. No workshop appointment, demonstration or access inspection has been arranged by Utkal. Agree the size, design, price and delivery terms before commissioning work. Ask separately about permission to share images of the work. A smaller piece with a story you understand can be a more lasting memory than a hurried purchase. If a pattern inspires a product of your own, discuss that use separately with the maker. Its torana, or ornamental gateway, is a separate structure in front of the temple. The official description identifies lion heads, makara motifs and bead-like ornament among the carvings on the arch. In Andrew Moore’s photograph above, the curve rests on two substantial pillars. The bands around the pillars, the figures above them and the projecting creatures give you several scales of detail to follow. First take in the whole opening; then choose one small part and see how it joins the rest. The gateway frames a view of the building beyond it. Looking through that frame is different from looking at the gateway itself. Give both a moment: the arch can hold your attention so completely that the temple behind it becomes a background.\"},{\"heading\":\"Two roofs, two spaces\",\"text\":\"Behind the torana are the shrine tower and the jagamohana, the hall in front of the shrine. Mukteswar’s hall has a stepped, pyramidal roof. The taller tower rises in a curving outline. These forms belong to the rekha and pidha vocabulary of Odisha’s temple architecture: the curving tower over the sanctum and the receding horizontal tiers over the hall. The distinction is also one of use. The sanctum houses the deity and is the focus of ritual worship; the hall provides a space before it where people can gather or wait. Once you recognise the pair, the building becomes a sequence of spaces rather than a single carved silhouette. Bikashrd’s side-view photograph below makes the contrast particularly clear. Follow the horizontal roof courses on the left, then the rising lines of the tower on the right. This is a way to read the photograph and the exterior; it does not depend on entering the shrine.\"},{\"heading\":\"Let a carving become a question\",\"text\":\"The temple’s decoration includes lattice windows and figures of ascetics worshipping a Shiva linga. These details place human action alongside repeated patterns: a figure performs an act, while a border or window repeats a shape. Look at posture, hands and the object a figure faces before asking for its name. What can you actually see? What becomes clearer when a guide identifies it? Keeping those two steps separate makes an explanation easier to follow and gives you something specific to ask about. A short visitor account cannot settle every carved scene or identify the people who made it. The sources used here place the temple broadly in the tenth century; they do not establish a named sculptor or a precise construction year for this guide.\"},{\"heading\":\"When the temple becomes a setting for Odissi\",\"text\":\"The Mukteswar Dance Festival brings Odissi to the temple precinct. The city’s visitor account dates the festival’s beginning to 1984 and describes solo, duet and group performances. It names Sujata Mohapatra, Aruna Mohanty, Ratikant Mohapatra and Madhvi Mudgal among artists who have performed there. That is a modern festival history. It does not by itself tell us which dances were performed at this particular temple a thousand years ago. A carved pose and a present-day performance may invite comparison, but the resemblance alone cannot establish an unbroken history. For a festival visit, find the organiser’s programme for the edition you intend to attend. Recurring descriptions are not a confirmed calendar: check the dates, performance times, venue arrangements and entry guidance before planning the evening.\"},{\"heading\":\"Leave room for worship and looking\",\"text\":\"Ask about entry, footwear and photography when you arrive, and ask before photographing people. Keep doorways clear while you study a detail. If steps or uneven ground are a concern, describe your needs before making a special trip; the photographs here cannot confirm today’s accessible route. Allow a temple visit and a performance evening their own time. For the daytime visit, one arch, one roof comparison and one carving are enough to give you questions to carry into the next temple. Dhauli preserves Major Rock Edicts I–X and XIV, with two Separate Rock Edicts. This is not the complete set of fourteen found elsewhere. When reading a translation, first check which edict and which site it represents. Major Rock Edict XIII, often quoted for its account of the Kalinga War, is absent at Dhauli. In Ven. S. Dhammika’s collection, the rendering of XIII follows the Kalsi version. Words about the war should not be mistaken for words carved on this particular rock.\"},{\"heading\":\"The people behind the proclamation\",\"text\":\"“All men are my children.” In Ven. S. Dhammika’s English rendering of the first Kalinga Rock Edict, Ashoka addresses the judicial officers at Tosali. The edict warns against unjust imprisonment and harsh treatment. It is an instruction to officials, not evidence that they always obeyed. That distinction matters: a proclamation tells us what the ruler wanted to declare, while the lives of the people governed by it are harder to recover. What would that promise have meant to someone waiting for a judgment? Keep the question beside the words.\"},{\"heading\":\"An elephant emerging from stone\",\"text\":\"The elephant’s front half emerges from the rock above the inscriptions. The city’s published recipe cooks the lentils and vegetables, adds a separate tempering in ghee, then finishes with roasted cumin and dried chilli ground to a powder. It lists either toor or moong dal and vegetables such as brinjal, yam and cauliflower. The name alone therefore does not tell you whether the bowl contains dairy or how it has been seasoned. Ask whether the kitchen is serving a fresh or fermented preparation, and which accompaniments come with it. Let that answer guide the rest of the order. Pakhala need not be treated as one more bowl alongside an already complete meal; you can make it the centre of lunch and choose the sides around it.\"},{\"heading\":\"Bhubaneswar at the table · Chhena poda: a sweet that keeps changing\",\"text\":\"Chhena poda is a baked chhena sweet. In a 2021 account, Bhubaneswar chef Michael describes making a chocolate version for the city’s .FEST celebration. His recipe mixes chocolate into the chhena before baking. It is a specific example of a cook adapting an Odia sweet, rather than proof that every version follows one fixed formula. The same account places the sweet’s beginnings in Nayagarh and retells the story of Sudarshana Sahoo leaving sweetened chhena in a warm oven. Read that as the origin story the chef recounts, not an independently established invention date. The documented modern adaptation is a different kind of evidence from the retrospective story. The photograph here was taken in Puri. Its browned edges and pale cut surfaces give you something concrete to compare when you encounter the dish yourself. The fruit and garnish belong to this photographed serving; they do not define how chhena poda must be presented.\"},{\"heading\":\"Bhubaneswar at the table · Korakhai and the life of Old Town\",\"text\":\"Old Town gives the meal a more local connection. Food here is part of worship and skilled work as well as something a visitor might buy. In her 2016 report, Sheela Pattanayak describes korakhai made with khai, sugar or jaggery, coconut and cardamom. Temple sevak Trinath Badu tells her that designated confectioner families prepare the Lingaraj offering. Shop owner Subash Sahu describes customers buying the sweet for themselves as well as for offerings. These are named accounts from that report, not new interviews. The distinction matters when you buy a packet: a sweet associated with a temple is not automatically a consecrated offering. Ask who made it and how it is intended to be used. Pick one bird you can see comfortably and note three things: its outline, the shape of its bill and how it moves. Is it walking, swimming, standing still or reaching into the water? Describe only what you can actually see. Then ask your guide which features support an identification. If two birds look alike, ask what separates them. Write down a local name as well, if one is offered, and the spelling your guide prefers. Leave a question mark when the view is too brief. A useful note might have spaces for the date, place, shape, action and possible name. Keep an observation such as “bill dipped into the water” separate from an explanation such as “feeding on fish” unless you saw the prey or have another reason for the conclusion. These are suggestions for your notebook, not observations recorded on a visit.\"},{\"heading\":\"Keep the birds’ attention elsewhere\",\"text\":\"Give feeding and resting birds room. The American Birding Association’s code asks birders to avoid stress, minimise habitat disturbance and use restraint with recordings and photography. These are general birding principles; follow the local guide’s access instructions and the rules that apply at Mangalajodi. For this outing, try listening without playing calls back to attract a bird. Use binoculars or a longer view instead of asking the boat to press closer. If the guide advises moving on, let an unfinished observation stay unfinished. Let others in the boat have time to look. Describe a bird’s position with a landmark that everyone can find, then wait while they locate it. Ask before recording your guide’s explanation, and credit them if they are comfortable being named.\"},{\"heading\":\"Arrange the pause as well as the trip\",\"text\":\"Before booking, agree the meeting point, length of the outing, price and return arrangements. In 2005, training by the Chilika Development Authority and Whale and Dolphin Conservation taught operators to turn engines off near dolphins and use long poles in shallow water; propeller guards were also encouraged. That is a historical training example, not proof of how a particular boat operates today. Before booking, ask how the operator avoids chasing, surrounding or cutting across dolphins, and what they do if several boats gather. Ask to see the guidance they follow. The season helps you plan; it cannot tell you which birds will be in front of you that morning. Keep a short record of the date, place and what you actually notice. If an identification is uncertain, leave it uncertain. A photograph or a few notes about shape and behaviour can become a useful question for a guide.\"},{\"heading\":\"People are part of the picture\",\"text\":\"Odisha Tourism describes Mangalajodi’s change from a place associated with bird poaching to one known for community conservation and guiding. Incredible India also describes local involvement in bird monitoring and habitat restoration. These accounts explain why meeting a guide is part of understanding the place, beyond finding birds. Ask how the wetland has changed during the years your guide has known it, and what conservation work involves today. Listen for particular examples. The broad story does not mean that every resident had the same past or that every tourism business supports conservation in the same way.\"},{\"heading\":\"Leave room for the birds\",\"text\":\"Watch from a distance that lets birds carry on feeding or resting. These suggestions follow the American Birding Association’s guidance on reducing disturbance; local access rules still apply. If you cannot get the photograph without moving closer, let the photograph go. Use binoculars if you have them, keep voices low and follow your guide’s advice about where to stop. Look at the photograph before you go. The open courtyard, shaded entrance and stepped blue roof give you a few details to recognise. It is a view from 2011, so leave room for changes rather than expecting the island to match it exactly.\"},{\"heading\":\"Jai’s journey\",\"text\":\"In Dr Janmejay Choudhury’s 2012 telling, a young bride named Jai crosses Chilika with her father on the way to her in-laws’ home. A storm wrecks the boat and she is lost. The account connects her memory with a protective goddess revered by people travelling on the lagoon. Choudhury quotes Godabarish Mishra’s poem Kalijai within his retelling. Read this as a story of belief and loss. It does not establish that a particular wreck happened, or that the shrine began with that event. The poem’s presence also matters: a printed retelling can carry literary language alongside a local tradition.\"},{\"heading\":\"A story is not a building date\",\"text\":\"The same essay also associates the deity with Parikuda’s royal household and proposes a different explanation of her name, Kalajayi. It does not establish a dated sequence between that account and Jai’s story. Neither explanation supplies a securely documented foundation date for the island shrine. If someone shares a version during your visit, ask where they first heard it and which details matter to them. Keep their words attached to their name, if they wish to be named. A new telling deserves to be heard in its own right, without being made to settle every question about the past.\"},{\"heading\":\"Leave time for the shrine\",\"text\":\"Agree on the departure shore, crossing, time ashore and return before leaving. Ask the operator about weather, boarding and correctly fitting lifejackets. Check the total price and what happens if the trip is cancelled. Current services and landing arrangements have not been confirmed here. At the shrine, ask about the current customs and where photography is welcome. Give worshippers space, and ask before photographing people. If someone in your group needs help with steps or balance, discuss boarding and access in advance. The lagoon’s connection with the Bay of Bengal is part of the attraction here, alongside the possibility of seeing Irrawaddy dolphins. A boat outing can be a way to understand that meeting of waters, rather than a race between stops. Before choosing a boat, ask the operator to describe the route: where you will leave from, which places you will pass, where you can go ashore and how long the return will take. A trip described simply as “Chilika” leaves too much unanswered.\"},{\"heading\":\"A glimpse can be enough\",\"text\":\"The Chilika Development Authority cautions that visitors rarely see an entire Irrawaddy dolphin. A head or part of the tail may be all that appears above the water. That modest expectation is useful: a brief view is still an encounter with a wild animal, and an outing may bring no sighting at all. Ask your guide what to watch for before the search begins. If you see something, describe its shape and direction instead of pressing for a closer approach. Leave time to watch the water after the first glimpse. You do not need a photograph to have noticed something.\"},{\"heading\":\"The space around a dolphin\",\"text\":\"Dolphin tourism also supports people who work on Chilika. The International Whaling Commission’s case study describes fishing boats adapted for visitors and income reaching local eateries and stalls. It also records concerns about engine noise, propellers and boats crowding the animals. The same activity can provide a livelihood and disturb the wildlife on which it depends. One practical response was a 2005 training programme run by Whale and Dolphin Conservation and the Chilika Development Authority. Operators were taught to turn engines off near dolphins and use poles to move slowly through shallow water. This is a documented example of changing boat practice, not proof that every trip follows it today. Before booking, ask how the operator avoids chasing, surrounding or cutting across dolphins. Make clear that you would rather keep a respectful distance than insist on a close photograph. A willingness to explain the approach matters more than a promise of a sighting.\"},{\"heading\":\"Make room for the shore\",\"text\":\"The district guide describes Satapada through fish and crabs as well as boats and dolphins. Arrange the practical details before leaving the shore: suitable lifejackets, help with boarding, the total price and the weather cancellation plan. Reading this history only as a succession of books would miss the part played by people voicing them. A list of literary names tells us where to begin; a scene can show what people do with words.\"]},{\"heading\":\"A song, then a primer\",\"text\":\"In Fakir Mohan Senapati’s story Rebati, the girl sits beside her father as he sings devotional songs and sometimes reads the Bhagabata. She learns songs by listening. Later, the teacher Basudev brings her a primer containing pictures of elephants, horses and cattle, and begins teaching her letters. Her father supports her learning; her grandmother objects, insisting that a girl should learn domestic work instead. The story brings two kinds of learning into the same household: remembering a song and learning to read a page. It also makes access to education a family argument. These are details of Senapati’s fiction, not evidence that every Odia household lived in the same way. They offer a specific question to carry into the story: who is encouraged to learn, and who is held back?\"]},{\"heading\":\"Choose a way to learn\",\"text\":\"For a structured introduction, CIIL’s catalogue lists Odia Language, Literature and Culture: An Introduction, edited by Sanjaya Kumar Bag and issued in 2019. Its stated audience is non-native learners, and its recorded language is Odia. A book’s intended audience and the language in which it teaches are both worth checking before choosing it. If you are beginning from spoken Odia, try reading a short passage with someone who can explain unfamiliar words. If you are beginning through English, keep the translator and edition beside the title. Hearing a passage, reading it in Odia and reading a translation offer different ways into the same work; none needs to stand for the whole language. The linked population atlas answers another question: how people’s mother tongues were recorded in a particular census. These different kinds of work offer useful context for reading him. A classroom, an account book and a household all involve authority: someone decides what is worth learning, what is owed and whose explanation will be believed.
