Geetashree Priyambada’s historical account connects his textbook writing with opposition to proposals to remove Odia from schools. A language needed books as well as arguments in its defence. Ramakanta Rout records that Senapati brought a printing press from Calcutta to Balasore in 1868, published Sambada Bahika and Bodhadayini, organised public meetings and wrote in Utkal Dipika. The account places him alongside other participants in the language movement. Textbooks gave pupils something to read; a press made more copies possible; journals carried arguments beyond a single classroom. Read together, these activities show how defending a language could involve the practical work of writing, printing and circulation.\",\"paragraphs\":[\"Odia’s place in school education was being challenged during Senapati’s lifetime. His educational and literary work belongs to the earlier foundations of that movement; the later province was a collective achievement.\",\"paragraphs\":[\"Odia-speaking regions were divided among several administrations. When he brings an illustrated primer, she turns its pages and shows the animal pictures to her mother and grandmother. Her grandmother wants her to learn cooking and household work instead. The wish to read is already part of a family conversation. The story later sets two explanations beside each other. After her parents die in an epidemic, the landlord’s men take the family’s cows for alleged arrears and withdraw its cultivation land. The grandmother blames Rebati’s education for their disasters. Yet the narrative has shown illness, lost income and dispossession. Details about food disappearing on fasting days unsettle the narrator’s elaborate defence of him. Praise becomes a way of making the reader suspicious. Chapter 10 turns the joke towards educated readers. Its narrator mocks men who can recite foreign genealogies but know little about their own neighbours. He explains the weavers’ community fund and then describes a village temple as a place of worship, public reading, meals and collective deliberation. To make those functions intelligible to his audience, he reaches for English labels: church, public library, hotel and town hall. The comparison reverses an expectation. A familiar village institution must apparently acquire English names before an educated reader can recognise its uses. The passage is an argument made by a fictional narrator, with its own defence of community authority. He invents a religious observance, persuades the servant Makara to lie under a covering in his place and goes out. When he returns intoxicated, Sulochana beats him with a broom; later she sees his injuries, regrets what she has done and tends him. In the closing exchange, Gopi Babu jokingly calls the beating a new remedy for his conduct. The story also describes the couple’s quieter life, reading Utkal Sahitya, Mukur and Dipika together. The movement from deception to violence, remorse and care makes an uneasy comedy. Read the wife’s authority alongside the demands of wifely devotion, and keep the injury in view when the narrator invites laughter.\",\"paragraphs\":[\"In Patent Medicine, Chandramani tries to escape his wife Sulochana’s restrictions on his outings. He then turns to inherited religious authority among the reader’s own people. The criticism changes direction. Customs dismissed as foolish in one community look less easy to dismiss when their logic appears closer to home. His interruptions matter. He addresses the reader, imagines objections and moves between an account of village life and an argument about the person reading it. Following the plot therefore also means asking what assumptions the narrator has caught us making.\"]},{\"heading\":\"Who gets heard in the courtroom?\",\"text\":\"The opening of the Cuttack Sessions Court chapter places Mangaraj before a crowded court. In the narrator’s satirical account, the judge ordinarily leaves much of the work to a subordinate while reading or writing letters. Patnaik’s reading draws attention to the people whose deaths a contest between royal families can leave out of view. The question here is not simply whether Sakuni succeeds. Ghosh uses Artaballabh Mohanty’s multi-volume edition, published from 1965, and explains that it draws on manuscripts with differing readings. His citations use pages rather than verse numbers. His study does not describe a single, settled critical text. An episode encountered in one edition therefore needs its edition details alongside it. The Government of Odisha’s Sarala Mahabharata catalogue offers numbered PDF downloads, giving readers a way to approach the Odia text. A catalogue label alone does not identify its relationship to Mohanty’s edition. Keep the file, parva, page and any editor or publication details with a passage before comparing it with a scholar’s account. Begin with one episode and stay with its choices: the destination of a prayer, the reason for a decision, the person left to bear its consequences. The poetry cannot settle those questions simply because its speaker describes suffering. Johannes Beltz makes this distinction central to his study of the poet’s remembered life. During fieldwork in western Odisha in 2000–2001, he collected stories from ascetics and lay people. He reads miraculous birth stories as evidence of how people honoured Bhima Bhoi, rather than as verified accounts of his birth. That leaves two worthwhile questions open: what can a document establish about a life, and what does a story reveal about the people who tell it? Read the image beside the account of the family’s work: losing the use of one’s land is also losing the time needed to live from it. Food, fire & the people behind a meal

Odisha cooks with fire

A blistered vegetable, an opened leaf parcel, a browned edge. Follow the heat into three food stories—and leave room for the cook’s own version.

Follow the heat ↗

Three methods. Many kitchen stories.

Begin the story ↓

Fire leaves different signatures. Start with roasted vegetables, then open a leaf parcel. Continue to baked dishes and notice how the method changes the story. These are documented preparations to explore, with real photographs and named accounts.

From flame to table

Start with the heat.

01 · Baigana poda

Beneath the blistered skin →

Follow eggplant from flame to mash, with a photograph that shows its tomato companion.

02 · Tomato poda · bilati baigana poda

A small bowl at the edge →

Find bilati poda beside pakhala, then ask which name and preparation the cook knows.

03 · Patrapoda

Open the parcel →

Mushroom, fish or prawn? The ingredient, leaf and cooking method each deserve a question.

Meet the maker

A good question
opens a kitchen story.

  • What is inside this preparation?
  • How is the heat used: direct roasting, a wrapped parcel, or baking?
  • Who taught you this version?

Leave room for another story

Follow the browned edge.

Continue to Poda pitha and Chhena poda. Their pages explain the preparations; a shared word does not make every cooking method the same.

Explore all food & flavours →
Poda pitha →Chhena Poda →

Which kitchen comes to mind?

Tell us about a preparation you know: its name, ingredients, method, place and the person who makes it. Share photographs and memories with permission.

Share a food memory →Open my journey →
Start a Fire and the Odisha table journey →The everyday Odisha table →Pakhala: build the rest of the meal →
Sources, image credits & editorial notes

A reading collection, not a fixed traditional meal, statewide origin claim or verified restaurant trail. Odia names and household variants await local review. The lead photograph combines eggplant and tomato. Each dish links to its own named sources. Human editorial and Odia review pending. Founder & Editor-in-Chief: Ahimanikya Satapathy.

  • Baigana-bilati poda: this photograph combines eggplant and tomato; it is not a photograph of the eggplant-only recipe. · Subhashish Panigrahi · CC BY-SA 4.0. Resized and converted to WebP; image remains under its stated licence.
  • Bilati poda is the red tomato dish at the left of this overhead pakhala meal, identified by photographer Subhashish Panigrahi, 2019. · Subhashish Panigrahi · CC BY-SA 4.0. Aspect-preserving resize and WebP compression; no scene alteration. Responsive display framing may crop the edges. Image remains CC BY-SA 4.0.
  • Fish patrapoda photographed in Rayagada. Mushroom and prawn preparations are discussed below but are not pictured. · Lopanayak · CC BY-SA 4.0. Resized and converted to WebP; image remains under its stated licence.
  • Poda pitha photographed by Udipta876; this serving does not represent every preparation. · Udipta876 · CC BY-SA 4.0. Aspect-preserving resize and WebP encoding; no creative edits. Display framing may crop edges. Resized image remains CC BY-SA 4.0.
  • A plated serving photographed in 2022: browned edges, a paler centre and added garnishes. · Subhransuphotography · CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikimedia Commons resized rendition; no creative edits.

Baigana podaବାଇଗଣ ପୋଡ଼ା

Roasted garlic or raw additions; flame or broiler.

By Ahimanikya Satapathy

Meet the dish ↗

A taste to remember. A question to take with you.

Begin the story ↓
Further readingFootnotes & Sources
On this page
Further readingFootnotes & Sources

Pragyan suggests putting garlic into slots in the eggplant before roasting. After peeling and mashing, roasted garlic, onion, ginger, cream and green chilli are added. The account also offers an oven alternative: this is one cook’s preparation, not a regional formula.1

Away in the Kitchen recalls a mother roasting eggplant and tomato over a flame. The writer adapts that preparation to a broiler, describing it as familiar but not smoky. The peeled vegetables are mashed with uncooked onion, garlic and chilli, then finished with mustard oil.2

The photograph shows combined eggplant and tomato, baigana-bilati poda. It is not a photograph of either recipe described here.

Food, fire & the people behind a meal

Odisha cooks with fire

A blistered vegetable, an opened leaf parcel, a browned edge. Follow the heat into three food stories—and leave room for the cook’s own version.

Follow the heat ↗

Three methods. Many kitchen stories.

Begin the story ↓

Fire leaves different signatures. Start with roasted vegetables, then open a leaf parcel. Continue to baked dishes and notice how the method changes the story. These are documented preparations to explore, with real photographs and named accounts.

From flame to table

Start with the heat.

01 · Baigana poda

Beneath the blistered skin →

Follow eggplant from flame to mash, with a photograph that shows its tomato companion.

02 · Tomato poda · bilati baigana poda

A small bowl at the edge →

Find bilati poda beside pakhala, then ask which name and preparation the cook knows.

03 · Patrapoda

Open the parcel →

Mushroom, fish or prawn? The ingredient, leaf and cooking method each deserve a question.

Meet the maker

A good question
opens a kitchen story.

  • What is inside this preparation?
  • How is the heat used: direct roasting, a wrapped parcel, or baking?
  • Who taught you this version?

Leave room for another story

Follow the browned edge.

Continue to Poda pitha and Chhena poda. Their pages explain the preparations; a shared word does not make every cooking method the same.

Explore all food & flavours →
Poda pitha →Chhena Poda →

Which kitchen comes to mind?

Tell us about a preparation you know: its name, ingredients, method, place and the person who makes it. Share photographs and memories with permission.

Baigana poda

By Ahimanikya Satapathy

Food · Across Odisha

Roasted garlic or raw additions; flame or broiler.

Confirm local access, transport and availability before travel.

Research checked 2026-11-06 · Editorial preview

Pragyan suggests putting garlic into slots in the eggplant before roasting. After peeling and mashing, roasted garlic, onion, ginger, cream and green chilli are added. The account also offers an oven alternative: this is one cook’s preparation, not a regional formula.

Away in the Kitchen recalls a mother roasting eggplant and tomato over a flame. The writer adapts that preparation to a broiler, describing it as familiar but not smoky. The peeled vegetables are mashed with uncooked onion, garlic and chilli, then finished with mustard oil.

The photograph shows combined eggplant and tomato, baigana-bilati poda. It is not a photograph of either recipe described here.
